title: Storage Estimation
summary: Sizing storage from one record's byte count to a multi-year total, including the replication and index overhead multipliers that turn a modest raw figure into the real footprint.

slides.markdown:
Storage estimation starts the same way every time: size one record, multiply by how many you'll have, then correct that raw figure for everything that isn't user data — replication, indexes, growth over time.

Skip any one of those steps and the number you hand an interviewer, or a capacity-planning doc, understates reality by 3-4x. This topic builds the full chain: one record, to a snapshot total, to a multi-year projection, to the real footprint after overhead.

slides.sectionTitle: From one record's size to total storage
slides.markdown:
Every storage estimate starts with one record: add up its fields — an ID (8 bytes), a text field, a timestamp (8 bytes), a bit of metadata — and round up generously, since you'll never guess every field a real schema ends up with.

For a short social post: user ID, ~100 bytes of text, timestamp, and metadata rounds to about **300 bytes/record**. With 500 million such records, total raw storage is 500,000,000 × 300 bytes = 150,000,000,000 bytes = **150 GB** (using 10^9 bytes/GB).

That's a snapshot at today's volume — the next slide adds the dimension that actually drives long-term capacity planning: growth.

A snapshot total tells you today's number; an interview or a capacity plan usually wants tomorrow's. Estimate a daily or yearly ingest rate, convert it to bytes, and project forward.

Say new records arrive at 10 million/day at 300 bytes each: that's 10,000,000 × 300 = 3,000,000,000 bytes/day ≈ **3 GB/day**. Over a year: 3 GB × 365 ≈ **1.1 TB/year**. Over 5 years: roughly **5.5 TB** of growth, on top of the 150 GB base from the previous slide — a total near **5.6 TB**.

The growth term usually dwarfs the starting snapshot within a few years — size for where the system will be, not where it is today.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: storage estimate worked example, line by line
slides.markdown:
![Vertical flow: record size 200 bytes, times 2 billion records equals 400 GB raw, times 3 replication equals final footprint 1.2 TB](assets/storage-estimate-flow.svg)

Take a chat application storing 2 billion messages at 200 bytes each: raw size is 2,000,000,000 × 200 = 400,000,000,000 bytes = **400 GB**. Apply a 3x replication factor for durability and the real footprint becomes 400 GB × 3 = **1.2 TB**.

Laying the steps out line by line — record size, raw total, each multiplier applied in order — is what keeps a storage estimate auditable instead of a single opaque number.

slides.sectionTitle: Don't forget the multipliers: replication factor, indexes, metadata
slides.markdown:
Raw data size is rarely what you actually provision. Three multipliers sit on top of it: **replication factor** (commonly 3x for durability — Cassandra and HDFS both default here), **secondary indexes** (each one adds roughly 10-30% depending on the fields indexed), and **storage-engine overhead** (write-ahead logs, per-row metadata, typically another 10-20%).

Worked together: 1 TB raw × 3 (replication) = 3 TB, then × 1.25 (a combined ~25% for indexes and metadata) = **3.75 TB** — the number to actually provision for, not the 1 TB you started with.

Treat replication and overhead as separate, compounding multipliers, not a single rough buffer.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: raw data size vs "real" storage footprint after overhead
slides.markdown:
Two numbers come out of the same estimate, and only one of them belongs on a purchase order.

| | Raw data size | Real storage footprint |
|---|---|---|
| What it counts | user-generated bytes only | raw x replication x index/metadata overhead |
| Example (1 TB raw) | 1 TB | ~3.75 TB (3x replication, 25% overhead) |
| Useful for | sanity-checking record-size assumptions | actual disk/cluster sizing |
| Common mistake | quoting this as the provisioning number | — |

**How to decide:** always report both — the raw figure shows your math is sane, the real footprint is the number that goes into a hardware or cost estimate.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: storage for a URL shortener over 5 years
slides.markdown:
Assumptions: 100 million new short links created per year, each record ~500 bytes (short code, long URL, metadata), 3x replication, 20% index overhead for the short-code lookup index.

```
Records after 5 years = 100,000,000/yr x 5 yr        = 500,000,000
Raw size              = 500,000,000 x 500 bytes       = 250,000,000,000 B
                                                        = 250 GB

With 3x replication    = 250 GB x 3                   = 750 GB
With 20% index overhead = 750 GB x 1.2                = 900 GB
```

Under 1 TB after 5 years is a genuinely small number — small enough that a single well-tuned instance could physically hold it, though you'd still replicate across machines for availability, not capacity.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: sizing storage but forgetting index and replica overhead
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "My data comes out to 250 GB, so a 250 GB disk covers it."

**Why it's wrong:** that 250 GB is raw data only. With standard 3x replication and roughly 20% index overhead — both essentially mandatory in a production system — the real requirement is closer to 900 GB, 3.6x higher. Provisioning for the raw figure means running out of disk, or discovering under-replicated data, the first time real load hits.

**Correct model:** always carry raw size through replication factor and index/metadata overhead before it becomes a hardware number. The raw figure is a sanity check, not a purchase order.
